A_target.statement:
Let $K \subseteq \R^n$ be [[Definition:Non-Empty Set|non-empty]], [[Definition:Compact Space|compact]] and [[Definition:Convex Set (Vector Space)|convex]], and $f: K \to K$ [[Definition:Continuous Mapping (Topology)|continuous]].
Then $f$ has a [[Definition:Fixed Point|fixed point]].

B_source.statement: Every continuous mapping of the closed unit ball $\Bbb D^n$ into itself has a fixed point.

substitutions.the ball: a large closed ball D containing K
substitutions.a self-map of the ball: f composed with the nearest-point retraction onto K

derived.a fixed point in the ball: a fixed point of f in K

object_map.reformulation: Extend f to a self-map of a ball by first retracting onto K; the fixed point property passes to retracts.

validity_conditions: For closed convex K the nearest-point map is well-defined and continuous (indeed 1-Lipschitz).
Any closed ball is homeomorphic to the unit ball, so the source result applies to it.
proof_plan:
Choose a closed ball $D \supseteq K$.
Let $r: D \to K$ send $x$ to the [[Definition:Nearest Point|nearest point]] of $K$; as $K$ is closed and convex, $r$ is a continuous [[Definition:Retraction (Topology)|retraction]].
Let $g = f \circ r: D \to D$, which is continuous with image in $K$.

By the source result, $\map g x = x$ for some $x \in D$.
Then $x = \map f {\map r x} \in K$, so $\map r x = x$.
